title: Bio & Health — September 26, 2026
summary: A thin edition: three developments cleared the evidence bar, spanning a new insulin approval, an early-stage viral enzyme finding, and evidence about industry influence on a tobacco rulemaking. Several research feeds were malformed or lacked independent coverage.

stories.headline: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approves Lilly's Onswik™ (insulin efsitora alfa-gobe), a once-weekly basal insulin injection treatment for adults living with type 2 diabetes
stories.dek: The approval adds a weekly basal insulin option for adults with type 2 diabetes; Lilly says its Phase 3 program included more than 3,400 participants.
tldr: The FDA approved Lilly's Onswik for adults with type 2 diabetes, according to the company's release and independent coverage.
Lilly says the approval relied on QWINT Phase 3 trials involving more than 3,400 adults and non-inferior A1C reductions versus daily basal insulins.
The approval is a product and regulatory milestone; this report offers no treatment advice.

body.text: Lilly announced FDA approval of Onswik, a once-weekly basal insulin indicated with diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes. The company says the QWINT Phase 3 program enrolled more than 3,400 adults and met its primary endpoint against daily basal-insulin comparators.

BioSpace reports the approval as a new competitive entry in the U.S. insulin market. Trial and label details should be read in the underlying regulatory materials; this edition does not infer adherence or clinical outcomes beyond the reported trial results.

stories.whyItMatters: The approval adds a longer dosing interval to Lilly's diabetes portfolio and creates a new product comparison point for the basal-insulin market, subject to labeling, access, and real-world uptake.
stories.editorNote: Headline is verbatim from Lilly's release. Company-reported trial facts are attributed; no efficacy guidance or patient recommendation is included.

stories.headline: Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?
stories.dek: The reported sequence pattern is a research lead; its biological function has not been established.
tldr: Anthropic says about 950 agents searched genomic data and identified a repeat pattern associated with reverse transcriptases in bacteriophages.
Nature reports that the sequence pattern resembles part of some CRISPR systems, but its function remains unknown and the preprint is not peer reviewed.
Anthropic says laboratory work to characterize the system is ongoing; no genome-editing tool or therapeutic application has been demonstrated.

body.text: Anthropic describes a computational search in which roughly 950 agents spent about 21 hours scanning genomic data and surfaced a repeated DNA pattern adjacent to reverse-transcriptase genes. The company calls the associated system array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART.

Nature notes that the pattern is structurally reminiscent of repeats in some microbial CRISPR systems, but there is scant evidence that it performs a similar function. The finding is in a preprint and remains an early lead pending characterization and peer review.

stories.whyItMatters: The episode illustrates a possible discovery workflow for AI-assisted genome mining while also showing the distance between surfacing a sequence pattern and demonstrating a biological mechanism or usable tool.
stories.editorNote: Headline is verbatim from Nature. Company's search scale is attributed to Anthropic; the story preserves Nature's uncertainty about function and peer review.

stories.headline: How Big Tobacco flooded the FDA with public comments to kill a menthol cigarette ban
stories.dek: A Rutgers analysis of FDA dockets found that most comments were form letters, with many traceable to tobacco-industry campaigns.
tldr: A Rutgers study of 246,808 comments on proposed FDA rules found that 97% of menthol-rule submissions were form letters.
The researchers linked a substantial share of those letters to tobacco-company campaigns, while only a small fraction were unique.
The study analyzes a past rulemaking record and does not establish that comment volume alone caused the FDA's decision.

body.text: STAT reports that the FDA received about 175,000 comments on its 2022 menthol proposal and that 97% were form letters, drawing on a Rutgers study published in JAMA Network Open. The study examined both menthol and flavored-cigar dockets.

The researchers' release says 46% of menthol-rule form letters contained material traceable to tobacco-company campaigns and that about 2% of comments were unique. The finding documents the composition of submissions; causal claims about the rule's eventual fate remain analysis rather than a measured experimental result.

stories.whyItMatters: The analysis shows how coordinated participation can shape the record agencies must evaluate, making comment provenance relevant to both public-health policy and regulatory process design.
stories.editorNote: Headline is verbatim from STAT. Study statistics are attributed to the Rutgers/JAMA research; causality is qualified.
